name: T-Bar Row
grip: Pronated or neutral closed grip on row handles.
description: Pull an angled lever row upward while lying prone on a chest-support pad, isolating the upper back musculature without lumbar strain.
setup: Adjust the footplate height so your chest rests comfortably against the upper angled pad (~45 degrees).
Lie face down with chest firmly supported and feet braced securely on the footrests.
Reach down to grasp the row handles with an overhand or neutral grip, extending arms fully to take up the load.
instructions: Pull the handles upward and backward toward your lower ribs or upper abdomen by driving elbows behind the torso.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top of the pull while keeping your chest glued to the pad.
Pause briefly at peak contraction without extending your lumbar spine or lifting off the pad.
Lower the weight under control until arms are fully extended and lats/rhomboids are comfortably stretched.
commonMistakes: Arching the back or lifting the sternum off the chest pad.
Using excessive momentum or jerking the lever at the start of the pull.
Failing to achieve full arm extension at the bottom.

logging.example: Two 20 kg plates on lever peg: record 40 kg total plate load.
logging.note: Chest-supported T-bar rows use pivoted lever arms with varying mechanical advantage; record loaded plate mass rather than free-weight barbell equivalent.

variantNote: Chest-supported incline T-bar machine variant (~45° pad angle), which eliminates lower-back shear compared to bent-over free-weight T-bar rows.
reviewNotes: Illustration depicts chest-supported variant to match modern commercial gym setups and eliminate lumbar fatigue.
